opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I don't think the boundary is where most people assume it is.

The usual intuition is that AI handles "pattern" problems and can't handle "deep" or "creative" ones. I think a more useful line is this: AI does well wherever a problem can be turned into a representation that is learnable from data, and where we can check whether the answer is right.

Take protein structure prediction. It looked like a profound physics problem, but it had three things going for it. There was a huge, well-curated dataset of solved structures. There was a clear objective, how close you get to the experimental structure. And the underlying physics constrained the space enough that a model could find the regularities. Once those three conditions hold, AI can represent the problem remarkably well, often better than our hand-built theories.

Where it gets hard is when one of those pillars is missing.

The first case is data. Some phenomena are rare, expensive to measure, or happen in regimes we've barely observed, like extreme materials conditions, many rare diseases, or early-universe physics. You can't learn a distribution you've never sampled. Simulation helps, but then you're learning your simulator's assumptions, not nature.

The second case is verification. If you can't tell whether the model's output is correct, you can't train it well and you can't trust it. A lot of frontier science is exactly this: the answer isn't known, and checking it requires a new experiment or a new conceptual framework.

The third case, which I find most interesting, is when the representation itself is the discovery. Much of the history of physics is someone inventing the right variables: entropy, fields, wavefunctions. Before those concepts existed, the problem wasn't just unsolved, it wasn't even properly stated. Current AI is very good at optimizing within a representation we hand it. It's much less clear that it can invent a fundamentally new one, a new language in which the problem suddenly becomes simple.

So I'd put the boundary roughly here. On one side are problems where we already know what to measure and what "correct" means, even if the mapping is extremely complex. AI is increasingly powerful there, and sometimes superhuman. On the other side are problems where the hard part is deciding what the relevant quantities are, or where nature has given us too few examples to generalize from. There, AI is a tool that assists humans rather than a replacement for scientific insight, at least for now.

That boundary isn't fixed, though. Every time we build better instruments, generate more data, or find a way to make a fuzzy question verifiable, we move problems from the second side to the first. In a sense, a big part of doing science in the AI era is exactly that work: turning problems AI can't yet represent into ones it can.

r001.rationale: It says problems must be turned into a representation learnable from data, but does not clearly state that the data itself must be converted into structured input.

r002.rationale: It discusses scarce or unobserved data and the difficulty of learning from it, but does not say that something unmeasurable cannot be represented by AI.

r003.rationale: It describes the representability boundary as a limitation of current AI generally, without restricting it to AI for Science.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, and I'll say upfront that I don't think the boundary is where most people assume it is.

The usual answer is that AI handles problems with lots of data and struggles with everything else. That's partly true but it misses the deeper point. What AI can represent well are problems that already have a formal structure, where we know what the variables are, what counts as a solution, and how to check an answer. Protein folding is the canonical example. The question was well-posed for fifty years. The space of inputs and outputs was clear. What was missing was a function that mapped one to the other, and that is exactly what large models are good at learning.

Where it gets harder is the kind of problem where the representation itself is the discovery. In my own field, before anyone found that twisting two graphene layers to a particular angle gives you superconductivity, the question didn't exist in a form you could feed to a model. Nobody was asking "what is the optimal twist angle." The insight was realizing that angle was a knob worth turning at all. AI is very good at optimizing within a space someone has already defined, and much weaker at noticing that the space is wrong, or that there's a dimension nobody has drawn yet.

There's a second boundary that I think is underappreciated, which is the relationship between the model and physical reality. In condensed matter, a huge fraction of the work is tacit. It's knowing that a sample looks slightly off under the microscope, that a measurement drifted because the cryostat is a bit humid, that a result is suspicious because of how the device was fabricated last Tuesday. That knowledge isn't written down anywhere. There's no corpus of it. So the model is reasoning about a cleaned-up version of the world, and the gap between that version and the lab is exactly where most of the actual science happens.

That said, I don't think these boundaries are fixed. The second one moves as we instrument labs better and as models start operating closed-loop with real experiments. The first one is more interesting to me, because I genuinely don't know if "proposing a new representation" is something that requires a certain kind of embodied intuition, or whether it's just a harder pattern that we haven't given models enough of the right examples to learn. If I had to bet, I'd say the boundary is less about what AI fundamentally can't do, and more about which parts of science we have bothered to make legible to it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI handles problems with formal structure, known variables, and clear inputs and outputs, which conveys that the problem’s data can be represented in structured form.

r002.rationale: It discusses tacit lab knowledge that is unwritten and missing from a model’s corpus, but does not state that anything unmeasurable cannot be represented by AI.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI’s limits in scientific examples, but does not identify the representability boundary as a general AI limitation beyond science.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between a problem AI can represent and a problem it can solve. You can write down an equation very compactly, but that doesn’t mean you can calculate its solution efficiently. And even if AI gives you a solution, that doesn’t necessarily mean it has explained the underlying physics.

For representation, the key question is whether you’ve captured the relevant information. What are the variables? What are the constraints? What do you leave out? If an important physical mechanism is missing, a more powerful model may fit the observations beautifully and still fail when conditions change.

So I wouldn’t draw a fixed line and say, ‘On this side are scientific problems AI can handle, and on that side are problems it never can.’ The boundary depends on our measurements, our mathematical language, and what we’re asking the model to do. Predicting an experimental result is different from discovering a principle that explains it.

The really interesting cases are where we don’t yet know the right representation. AI might help us find one. But we still need experiments to establish whether that representation captures something real.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representing relevant information through variables and constraints, but does not state that data must be convertible into structured input.

r002.rationale: It mentions measurements as one factor in where the boundary lies, but does not say that unmeasurable things cannot be represented by AI.

r003.rationale: The response describes a boundary that depends on measurements, mathematical language, and the task; it does not identify representability as a general AI limitation rather than one specific to AI for Science.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the boundary is less between particular fields of science and more between what we can formulate clearly and what we don’t yet know how to formulate. If we can specify the relevant variables, the constraints, and what counts as a good prediction, AI has something concrete to work with. But in many scientific problems, discovering the right variables is itself the breakthrough.

There’s also a distinction between representing a phenomenon and understanding it. A model might predict an experimental result very accurately without telling us which mechanism produces it. To establish that mechanism, we still need experiments that distinguish competing explanations.

So I wouldn’t draw a permanent line and say, ‘AI can do this, but it can never do that.’ I’d ask: What information does it have? What assumptions are built into its representation? And how can we test its answer? The boundary can move as our measurements and concepts improve, but expressing an answer is only the beginning of demonstrating that it’s scientifically meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can work with a problem when its relevant variables, constraints, and prediction goals can be specified, which communicates the need for a structured formulation.

r002.rationale: The response says measurements and concepts can improve, but does not state that anything unmeasurable cannot be represented by AI.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI representation in scientific problems, but does not identify the boundary as a general limitation of AI rather than one specific to AI for Science.
